This post is part of the [Image Registration Series](index.qmd) series.
:::

Five methods, one benchmark, ground-truth pixel error throughout. Here's everything from
[Part 1](01-classical-methods.qmd), [Part 2](02-dl-affine-and-feature-matching.qmd), and
[Part 3](03-dl-deformable-registration.qmd) side by side, plus the question that actually started
this series: which of these are you allowed to ship in a company's product.

## Head-to-head results

| Method | Type | Scenario A (affine) | Scenario B (affine+elastic) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase correlation | Classical, translation-only | 10.23 px | 10.21 px |
| ECC (affine) | Classical, intensity-based | **0.02 px** | 0.21 px |
| SIFT + RANSAC | Classical, feature-based | 0.05 px | 0.20 px |
| DL affine CNN | Deep learning, learned regressor | 5.26 px | 5.26 px |
| LoFTR + RANSAC | Deep learning, deep feature matching | 0.04 px | 0.19 px |
| VoxelMorph-style, single network on raw drift | Deep learning, deformable | 9.99 px | 10.02 px |
| **VoxelMorph-style, ECC affine + residual network** | Deep learning, two-stage deformable | 0.38 px | **0.41 px** |

Four things stand out:

1. **On pure affine drift, classical intensity-based (ECC) and feature-based (SIFT+RANSAC)
   optimization are already essentially perfect** -- sub-pixel, no training data, no GPU. Nothing
   here beat them; LoFTR tied them.
2. **The DL method that replaces the optimizer (the affine CNN) underperformed the DL method that
   replaces the feature detector (LoFTR) by roughly two orders of magnitude** on this benchmark.
   That's not a general law about deep learning and registration -- it's a statement about how much
   harder "learn to regress a precise transform end to end from a small dataset" is than "learn
   generically useful local correspondences," at the model sizes and training budgets used here.
3. **Only a deformable network can touch Scenario B's non-rigid component at all** -- every
   affine-only method, classical or deep, hits a hard representational ceiling there, by
   construction, regardless of how well-trained or well-optimized it is. But *asking one dense-field
   network to also absorb a large rigid component first is a real, measured mistake* (9.99-10.02px)
   -- chaining classical affine pre-alignment in front of a residual-only deformable network fixed
   it completely (0.38-0.41px, competitive with the best classical methods). This is standard
   practice in the actual literature, not a workaround invented for this post.
4. **The best non-rigid result in the series is a hybrid**: one classical method (ECC) doing what
   it's already excellent at, feeding a small deep network that only ever has to learn the part
   ECC structurally cannot represent.

## Licensing: code license and weights license are two different questions

This is the question that started the series, and it deserves the same rigor as the accuracy
numbers above: a permissive **code** license does not automatically mean the **pretrained weights**
are equally free to use in a company product. Always check both, separately.

| Method | Code license | Pretrained weights | Commercial/company use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase correlation, ECC (OpenCV) | Apache License 2.0 | n/a (no learned weights) | **Yes** |
| SIFT (OpenCV `cv2.SIFT_create`) | Apache License 2.0 | n/a | **Yes** -- SIFT's original US patent (6,711,293) expired March 2020; OpenCV moved it out of the patent-encumbered `opencv-contrib` "nonfree" module into the main package after that |
| VoxelMorph (original) | Apache License 2.0 | Apache License 2.0 | **Yes** |
| TransMorph | Permissive (MIT-style) | Permissive (MIT-style) | **Yes** -- verify the exact license file in the specific repo/version you pull, since terms can change between releases |
| LoFTR (via kornia) | Apache License 2.0 | Apache License 2.0 (`pretrained="outdoor"`/`"indoor"`) | **Yes** |
| MONAI registration modules | Apache License 2.0 | Apache License 2.0 | **Yes** |
| ANTs / ANTsPy, elastix/SimpleElastix | Apache License 2.0 | n/a (classical, no learned weights) | **Yes** |
| **SuperPoint / SuperGlue** (Magic Leap) | **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** | **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** | **No** -- non-commercial, share-alike; needs a separate commercial license from Magic Leap for company use |

The one to actually remember: **SuperGlue/SuperPoint is everywhere in registration and SLAM
papers, tutorials, and demo repos, and it is not licensed for company work.** LoFTR (used in
[Part 2](02-dl-affine-and-feature-matching.qmd)) is the practical, Apache-2.0, commercially-clean
way to get the same category of deep feature matching.

The general trap worth internalizing beyond this specific table: a repo's top-level `LICENSE` file
covers the *code*. Pretrained checkpoints are sometimes released under different terms in the same
repo (a separate `MODEL_LICENSE`, a clause in the README, or -- worse -- silence, which legally
defaults to "all rights reserved" and needs the author's explicit permission), and a checkpoint
trained on a restricted dataset can carry that dataset's redistribution restrictions even when the
training *code* is Apache/MIT. **When a company's legal/compliance process asks "is this okay to
ship," "the GitHub repo is Apache 2.0" is an incomplete answer** -- confirm the weights file's terms
separately, and when a checkpoint's provenance is unclear, the safe move is retraining a
permissively-licensed architecture (VoxelMorph, TransMorph, LoFTR/kornia are all good bets here) on
your own data instead of trusting an unlabeled checkpoint.

## The recommendation

For a semiconductor inspection pipeline correcting stage/fixture drift:

- **If the drift is purely rigid/affine (the common case for stage repeatability)**: use **ECC or
  SIFT+RANSAC**. Both are sub-pixel accurate on this benchmark, need no training data or GPU, are
  fully permissively licensed, and are simpler to validate and maintain than a trained model. This
  is not a close call -- there is no accuracy reason to reach for deep learning here.
- **If you need deep feature matching anyway** (e.g. the imaging conditions vary enough that a
  learned matcher's robustness is worth it, or you're already standardized on a DL stack): use
  **LoFTR via kornia**, not SuperGlue/SuperPoint -- same job, same accuracy tier on this benchmark,
  actually licensed for the work.
- **If the drift has a real non-rigid/local component** (thermal drift, fixture flex, anything a
  single affine matrix structurally can't represent): **don't hand a deformable network the raw
  drifted image and expect it to do everything.** Run classical affine pre-alignment (ECC) first,
  then a VoxelMorph-style network trained only on the residual local warp -- this series' own
  numbers show that split is worth roughly 25x the accuracy of a single network trying to do both
  jobs at once. The deformable stage, and the practical architectures around it (SynthMorph,
  TransMorph), are Apache/MIT licensed and safe to build on.
- **Don't train a small from-scratch affine regressor as a first move.** This series' own DL affine
  CNN (5.26px) badly underperformed classical optimization on a problem ECC already solves to
  sub-pixel accuracy with less code and no training pipeline to maintain -- and it wasn't even the
  weakest deep-learning number in this series, since asking one network to do affine *and*
  deformable correction together (Part 3's first attempt) did worse still (~10px). **The general
  shape of every failure in this series is the same: a deep model doing a job a purpose-built
  classical method already does better.**

The pattern across the whole series: **reach for deep learning where it earns its complexity --
non-rigid deformation, or matching robustness under real visual variation -- not as a default
replacement for a classical method that already works.**
